sleep-clock-01.text: Those calculations can become another demand. If practical, turn the clock away and give the numbers a rest.

sleep-clock-04.text: You do not need to keep updating that number. Settle into what is comfortable and leave the calculation alone.

sleep-clock-05.text: A score cannot describe your whole night or day. Notice how you feel without making the number another target tonight.

sleep-clock-03.text: Could the clock face be out of view while the alarm stays set? You can stop supervising each minute.

sleep-clock-08.text: Being awake is not a failure. Take some pressure off the task of sleeping and choose a calmer next moment.

sleep-clock-07.text: Sleep is not something you can guarantee on a timer. We can make the next ten minutes quieter and more comfortable.

sleep-clock-06.text: Treat the tracker as one imperfect piece of information. Your own experience matters too; it does not need to match every estimate.

sleep-clock-09.text: Different people have different nights. Focus on what helps your own rest, rather than matching someone else's pattern.

sleep-waking-01.text: Keep this visit simple. You can listen briefly, then put the screen away without opening anything else.

sleep-clock-10.text: You can stop testing the feeling. Let a quiet activity or the support beneath you have some attention instead.

sleep-waking-04.text: If one thing needs remembering, make a brief note. The rest of the thinking can wait for daylight.

sleep-waking-03.text: Look around and notice where you are now. You do not have to interpret the dream before settling again.

sleep-waking-02.text: Do not force it. If lying awake feels frustrating, a quiet activity in dim light may feel easier until you are sleepy.

sleep-waking-05.text: Choose a recording, then turn away from the screen. You do not need to watch Luma to listen.

sleep-waking-07.text: Those messages can wait unless something truly needs you. Let the night stay separate from the inbox.

sleep-waking-06.text: You do not need to start solving the whole day yet. Decide whether a quiet rest or a gentle beginning feels more useful.

sleep-waking-10.text: Yes. Let this be a little quiet company. You do not have to produce sleep by the end of the recording.

sleep-waking-08.text: You did not choose to be awake. Leave the criticism out and make the next few minutes less demanding.

sleep-waking-09.text: Choose something quieter for now. A demanding workout can wait for a time when you are prepared and able to exercise comfortably.

sleep-noise-02.text: That is frustrating when you need rest. Choose a practical comfort now, and leave any longer conversation for a better time.

sleep-noise-01.text: If you can, ask for one specific change, such as headphones or a lower screen brightness. Keep the request simple.

sleep-noise-04.text: It may help to discuss a different alarm arrangement together. Look for a practical adjustment, rather than blaming either person's schedule.

sleep-noise-05.text: You do not have to like the sounds. Try letting one steady sensation, such as the bedding, share your attention.

sleep-noise-03.text: You can have a different rhythm from the room around you. Is there a quieter place or a small boundary you can choose?

sleep-noise-07.text: Then silence is the right choice for now. End the recording whenever you like; there is no final instruction to wait for.

sleep-noise-08.text: Keep your next step small and practical. You can choose quiet movement without making yourself hold an uncomfortable position.

sleep-noise-06.text: You can try the soft rustling in the resting space. Keep it comfortable and switch it off if quiet feels better.

sleep-noise-10.text: Choose a calm time away from bedtime. Describe one difficulty and one adjustment you would like to try together.

sleep-noise-09.text: Your rest can follow your own needs. A familiar wind-down can begin even while someone else's evening continues.

sleep-away-01.text: Notice a few ordinary details, then make one part of the space comfortable. You do not have to feel completely at home.

sleep-away-02.text: Let arriving be enough for a moment. Put down your bags and choose comfort before catching up with everything.

sleep-away-04.text: Give yourself permission to ask for an ordinary need, such as water, another blanket, or somewhere to charge your phone.

sleep-away-03.text: Keep the smallest familiar part of it. A routine can travel in pieces; it does not need all its usual conditions.

sleep-away-06.text: Travel can disrupt your rhythm. Keep the next step gentle; if sleep problems persist, ask a healthcare professional for advice.

sleep-away-05.text: Check your essential arrangements once, then put the plan somewhere visible for morning. Rechecking does not need to fill the whole night.

sleep-away-08.text: That familiar comfort matters. You can acknowledge missing it while making this resting place a little easier for tonight.

sleep-away-10.text: Find a supported position, let your hands rest, and notice the room. Nothing special needs to be packed for that.

sleep-away-09.text: You can ask for a small amount of privacy or quiet. An ordinary need does not require a complicated explanation.

sleep-shifts-03.text: You could explain your rest window and adjust nonessential notifications. Keep any genuinely important contacts reachable.

sleep-shifts-02.text: You have been alert for a long stretch. Make the next part quieter and simpler, without expecting an instant switch into sleep.

sleep-shifts-01.text: Your schedule needs room for your actual working hours. Start with a repeatable settling routine around the sleep opportunity you have.

sleep-shifts-04.text: A fixed clock time may not fit. Keep a few familiar wind-down steps that can move with your schedule.

sleep-shifts-06.text: Do not drive while too sleepy to do so safely. Arrange another way home or stop somewhere safe to rest.

sleep-shifts-05.text: Your rest does not become less necessary because it happens in daylight. You are responding to the hours you worked.

sleep-shifts-08.text: Use the sleep journal for the time you actually rested. Your night does not have to match a conventional bedtime.

sleep-shifts-09.text: Protect the rest that is possible without making the gap another performance. Consider whether someone can help with a practical demand.

sleep-small-routine-02.text: A short visible list can hold the order for you. Keep only the steps that make the evening easier.

sleep-small-routine-01.text: Choose one familiar cue and one comfort: put the phone aside, then settle somewhere supported. You can build from there.

sleep-shifts-10.text: Check whether you are still responsible for responding, then quiet what you can. Let your next moment ask less of you.

sleep-small-routine-05.text: Make a small version in advance. Keep the essentials and one comfort, so tiredness does not require fresh planning.

sleep-small-routine-04.text: Of course. Choose a quiet activity you actually enjoy; meditation is only one option for winding down.

sleep-small-routine-03.text: Remove one unnecessary step. The routine is there to support rest, not to create another way to fall behind.

sleep-small-routine-06.text: You do not need one. Notice what supports your rest without turning every evening into a score.

sleep-small-routine-08.text: Choose a closing action for work and a different first action for rest. Make the boundary visible, even if it is small.

sleep-small-routine-07.text: Use a flexible beginning rather than a perfect time. Even one quiet transition after their needs are met can belong to you.

sleep-small-routine-09.text: It does not have to. Familiar elements can help without requiring your life to repeat the same script.

sleep-resting-daytime-01.text: If your situation allows it, take the rest you need. You do not have to justify every quiet moment with exhaustion.

sleep-small-routine-10.text: That step still counts as care. You can keep the routine small enough to use again, rather than judging what was missing.

sleep-resting-daytime-04.text: Choose a comfortable place and a reliable reminder if you need to leave at a certain time. Keep the pause simple.

sleep-resting-daytime-02.text: Yes. You can choose a comfortable, low-demand pause without setting sleep as the outcome.

sleep-resting-daytime-07.text: Put the chores somewhere outside your head. You can choose whether to return to them after the pause.

sleep-resting-daytime-06.text: A smaller break may still be possible. Step away from the task briefly and choose a comfortable change of position.

sleep-resting-daytime-05.text: Persistent tiredness is worth discussing with a healthcare professional. An app cannot work out the cause from a brief conversation.

sleep-resting-daytime-08.text: You do not need the right furniture to rest. Choose what feels comfortable and practical in your situation.

sleep-resting-daytime-09.text: You can leave those minutes unfilled. Pick one comfortable place and let that be the plan.

sleep-resting-daytime-10.text: Give yourself a little time to become alert before demanding tasks. Avoid driving or risky activities while you still feel too sleepy.

sleep-journal-help-01.text: Open Sleep and choose Log your sleep. Review the bedtime, wake time and how you felt before saving.

sleep-journal-help-03.text: Choose the relevant date in the sleep journal and review the entry before saving it. Keep uncertain details clearly approximate.

sleep-journal-help-02.text: Use an honest estimate if the journal asks for a time. You do not need to invent precision you do not have.

sleep-journal-help-04.text: Open the saved sleep entry and edit the time. Check the date as well before saving your correction.

sleep-journal-help-05.text: You can choose how much to record. The journal should support noticing your rest, not make you grade every night.

sleep-journal-help-09.text: Your experience is useful information too. Note how you felt and keep any timing estimates honest.

sleep-journal-help-08.text: You can resume with the next night you remember. There is no need to reconstruct missing nights to make the record look complete.

sleep-journal-help-07.text: Record the experience as accurately as the journal allows, and add a note about the separate stretches rather than implying uninterrupted sleep.

sleep-alarm-help-02.text: Review the alarm time and day before saving. For waking with Daywell closed, set the alarm in your phone's clock as well.

sleep-alarm-help-01.text: No. Browser alarms need Daywell open. Use your phone's built-in alarm for a dependable wake-up while the app is closed.

sleep-journal-help-10.text: Look back through your saved days for repeated patterns and context. Avoid treating one unusually good or bad night as the whole story.

sleep-alarm-help-03.text: Choose a sound and volume that suit you in your device's alarm settings. Daywell cannot change those settings for you.

sleep-alarm-help-05.text: Check the saved alarm list for the time you intended. This recording alone cannot confirm that an alarm was saved.

sleep-alarm-help-04.text: In Sleep, choose Adjust schedule and review the new wake-up time. A preference is separate from a reliable device alarm.

sleep-alarm-help-06.text: Check the alarm controls available in your device's clock. Review each day's setting rather than assuming a repeat schedule was created.

sleep-alarm-help-07.text: Set a reliable device alarm and prepare what you need. After checking once, let the reminder carry some of the remembering.

sleep-alarm-help-08.text: I cannot control your phone's snooze button. You could make the first morning action small and place the alarm where you can reach it safely.

sleep-alarm-help-10.text: Plan a small first step rather than a whole perfect morning. Leave a little room before the day's demands, if you can.

sleep-alarm-help-09.text: The browser may pause when closed or suspended. Use the device clock for essential alarms and keep Daywell open for its timers.

sleep-late-screen-03.text: You can put it down after this sentence. There is no reward waiting at the end of the feed.

sleep-late-screen-01.text: Choose what you want the phone to do before you lie down. A single recording can end without opening the feed.

sleep-late-screen-02.text: You could try audio with a clear ending. It can offer company without asking your eyes to follow another video.

sleep-late-screen-06.text: Choose a concrete ending, such as closing the current page. Do not wait for the internet to run out of things to show you.

sleep-late-screen-04.text: If nothing urgent requires you, leave the inbox for your next work period. Bedtime does not need to become an extra shift.

sleep-late-screen-05.text: Start the recording, then turn the screen away if that suits you. You do not have to watch the app.

sleep-late-screen-07.text: Keep essential contacts available and quiet the rest if practical. You do not need every update in order to be reachable.

sleep-late-screen-08.text: Daywell cannot lock your phone. Device screen-time or focus settings may offer the boundary you want.

sleep-late-screen-09.text: You can change the next moment without shaming the last one. Put the phone down and choose one small comfort.

sleep-after-short-night-02.text: Punishment will not return the lost rest. Choose a practical adjustment that makes today a little easier.

sleep-after-short-night-01.text: A short night can make the day harder, but you can still adjust the plan. Start with what is essential.

sleep-late-screen-10.text: Notice whether that is what you want or simply the next habit. You can let the recording be the last screen activity tonight.

sleep-after-short-night-05.text: Lower the demands where you can. You can be honest that today needs a little more care and patience.

sleep-after-short-night-04.text: Separate essentials from preferences. Move one nonurgent item if possible, and leave room for ordinary needs.

sleep-after-short-night-03.text: Consider a gentler option or rest, especially if you feel unwell or too sleepy. You do not need to prove anything today.

sleep-after-short-night-08.text: One night does not tell the whole story. Look for a longer pattern before changing everything at once.

sleep-after-short-night-07.text: Write what happened in ordinary language. The journal is a record of your experience, not a grade for how well you slept.

sleep-after-short-night-06.text: Do not drive while struggling to stay awake. Arrange another way to travel or rest somewhere safe before reconsidering.

sleep-after-short-night-10.text: Make the next task smaller. You can begin with the necessary part and leave extra polish for another day.

move-first-step-01.text: Make the first action tiny: put on comfortable shoes or clear a little space. You can decide the rest afterwards.

sleep-after-short-night-09.text: It is okay to name that you are tired. Then choose one concrete way to support yourself through the next part of the day.

move-first-step-04.text: Try one of the gentle routines in Move. Read the first step before deciding whether it fits today.

move-first-step-03.text: Beginning is a place to start, not something to hide. Choose a movement you can learn at a comfortable pace.

move-first-step-02.text: Start gently and build gradually. If you have health concerns or have been inactive for a long time, check with a clinician first.

move-first-step-07.text: Look at First steps strength in Move. Start within your comfort and get qualified guidance if the movements are unfamiliar.

move-first-step-05.text: You could try the smallest practical beginning before motivation arrives. Opening the routine can be that beginning.

move-first-step-06.text: The clothes can wait without becoming a judgment. Choose one short, comfortable activity you actually want to try.

move-first-step-10.text: Then you did one exercise. You can learn from how it felt without treating a shorter session as failure.

move-first-step-09.text: You can start smaller than the plan in your head. A manageable beginning is easier to return to.

move-first-step-08.text: It can make the next step easier. Notice the preparation, then choose whether a little movement fits right now.

move-short-window-02.text: A short session is still movement. Choose something that fits the time you actually have.

move-short-window-01.text: Five minutes can be a real opportunity. The Desk break routine offers a simple place to start.

move-short-window-03.text: You can choose a smaller version or a short walk. The day does not need an all-or-nothing decision.

move-short-window-05.text: Choose a routine that leaves time to settle afterwards. The gap does not need to be filled to its last second.

move-short-window-04.text: Keep an eye on the cooking and choose something safe nearby. Do not leave a hot stove unattended to exercise.

move-short-window-06.text: You can use smaller opportunities when they fit. Notice what is practical, rather than waiting for one perfect long session.

move-short-window-07.text: Pick a gentle activity with a clear ending. Leave yourself a little time to become comfortable for the call.

move-short-window-08.text: Make the planned session shorter before the next attempt. A plan that fits your life is easier to use.

move-short-window-09.text: If comfortable, stand or shift position and move gently. Keep the movement suited to your body and surroundings.

move-desk-pause-01.text: If you can, take a short movement break now. Change position and choose a comfortable way to move.

move-short-window-10.text: Half a walk still happened. Record what you actually did, if you want, and leave out the punishment for the rest.

move-desk-pause-02.text: Try an easier position and a gentle movement within comfort. Do not force a stretch or push into pain.

move-desk-pause-03.text: Choose a gentle routine or a short easy walk. A break does not need to become a workout.

move-desk-pause-05.text: That can be a useful cue. If it is practical, step away for a comfortable movement while you wait.

move-desk-pause-04.text: A brief change of position may still fit. Keep it safe and comfortable within the space you have.

move-desk-pause-06.text: Link a movement pause to something you already notice, like finishing a call. A reliable device reminder is another option.

move-desk-pause-07.text: Choose a supported position and movements already comfortable for you. For tailored seated exercises, ask a qualified professional.

move-desk-pause-08.text: Start with a gentle change of position. Give yourself room to move without trying to undo the whole day at once.

move-desk-pause-10.text: Before leaving, note the next task step. That can make returning easier after your movement break.

move-walk-choice-01.text: Choose a simple route and put on your shoes. You do not need to decide on a perfect distance first.

move-walk-choice-03.text: You can walk without a number. Choose the route or time that suits you and let the movement be enough.

move-walk-choice-04.text: A familiar, comfortable route may make the start easier. You can also invite someone, without waiting for company every time.

move-walk-choice-02.text: Pick somewhere familiar and safe for your circumstances. A short route you already know can reduce the decisions.

move-walk-choice-07.text: Then leave the targets out. You can notice the surroundings and return when it feels practical.

move-walk-choice-05.text: Yes. Choose a pace that fits your comfort and situation. A walk does not have to become a competition.

move-walk-choice-06.text: If it suits you, choose a comfortable route and pace. The After-meal stroll routine can keep the plan simple.

move-walk-choice-08.text: That was still movement in your day. You can record it without pretending it was a different kind of session.

move-walk-choice-10.text: I do not have a verified local route here. Use a trusted map and check the route's suitability for your circumstances.

move-walk-choice-09.text: Keep your attention on the route and surroundings. Leave the screen and any inward-focus exercise until you are safely stopped.

move-weather-plan-03.text: Choose a safer option rather than keeping the walk at any cost. An indoor movement break may be enough today.

move-weather-plan-01.text: You can choose an indoor alternative or a shorter plan. Weather changing the activity does not erase your intention.

move-weather-plan-02.text: Adjust or postpone the session if conditions are uncomfortable. A gentler indoor option may fit better than forcing the original plan.

move-weather-plan-06.text: It is reasonable to change the plan. Pick another activity or wait for safer conditions.

move-weather-plan-05.text: Choose an activity that feels comfortable in the room you have. You can reduce the intensity or take a rest instead.

move-weather-plan-04.text: Consider a well-lit familiar route, a different time, or an indoor activity. Your comfort and safety matter more than the exact plan.

move-weather-plan-07.text: Look through the no-equipment routines in Move. Choose one that suits your space and current ability.

move-weather-plan-09.text: Use a current local forecast before deciding. This recording cannot check live weather or tell you conditions are safe.

move-weather-plan-08.text: You can make a practical decision without judging it. Ask whether an indoor option fits, or whether today calls for rest.

move-small-home-02.text: Try the Quiet living-room cardio routine. Read each movement and adapt or skip anything unsuitable for your space.

move-weather-plan-10.text: Choose one indoor option in advance. A simple backup can save you from making the whole decision again on a difficult day.

move-small-home-01.text: Check the space needed for each movement before starting. Choose a smaller, safe option rather than forcing the routine into a cramped area.

move-small-home-04.text: Clear only the safe space needed before moving. If that is not possible, choose another activity or place.

move-small-home-03.text: Several Move routines need no equipment. Start with one that matches your experience and the room available.

move-small-home-05.text: Only use equipment that is stable and suitable for the movement. If unsure, choose a no-equipment exercise or ask for qualified guidance.

move-small-home-06.text: Choose quiet, controlled movements and a practical time. You can keep the session gentle and short.

move-small-home-08.text: Open Move and choose No equipment or Around the house. Read the routine and check the space before beginning.

move-small-home-07.text: Skip floor-based movements. Choose an accessible alternative and seek tailored guidance if you need help finding suitable exercises.

move-small-home-09.text: Pause and make the area safe before continuing. You do not need to finish a set while avoiding an obstacle.

move-gym-confidence-01.text: Give the first visit a small purpose, such as learning the layout. You do not have to master everything on arrival.

move-small-home-10.text: Find a safe space and choose a brief activity that fits. It is also okay to wait for a less crowded moment.

move-gym-confidence-02.text: Ask a qualified member of staff to show you. It is better to learn the setup than guess under load.

move-gym-confidence-04.text: That feeling can be uncomfortable. Keep your attention on one familiar exercise and ask staff for support if it would help.

move-gym-confidence-03.text: You can wait, choose a suitable alternative you know, or shorten the session. The exact order is not a test.

move-gym-confidence-07.text: Choose a session that works safely with what you have. You do not need to improvise a risky replacement.

move-gym-confidence-06.text: Learning the equipment is a reasonable reason to ask. A short question can make your session clearer and safer.

move-gym-confidence-05.text: The Gym full body routines give a starting structure. Get instruction for unfamiliar movements and choose loads appropriate to your experience.

move-gym-confidence-09.text: Their training is not your instruction. Choose a load you can control with the technique you have learned.

move-gym-confidence-08.text: You can decide what fits today. A short visit can still help you learn what would make the next one easier.

move-gym-confidence-10.text: No. This recording cannot see your technique. Ask a qualified coach for feedback on the movement you are doing.

move-strength-basics-02.text: It means eight repetitions, then a rest, repeated for three sets. The movement and load still need to suit you.

move-strength-basics-01.text: A rep is one repetition of a movement. A set is a group of those repetitions before you rest.

move-strength-basics-03.text: Learn movements you can control, keep the effort appropriate, and build gradually. Consistency can be a gentler goal than constant increases.

move-strength-basics-06.text: Yes, bodyweight movements can be part of strength work. Choose versions suitable for your current ability and comfort.

move-strength-basics-04.text: No. Start with learning the movement and an appropriate level of resistance. Qualified guidance can help you choose.

move-strength-basics-05.text: Use a simple note or the routine's set display. You do not need to hold the whole session in memory.

move-strength-basics-09.text: Consider your experience, comfort and any health limits. A qualified professional can help if you are unsure about a specific movement.

move-strength-basics-08.text: Choose one movement at a time. Learn what that movement asks of you before worrying about the rest of the vocabulary.

move-strength-basics-07.text: Start with a manageable strength routine and regular nourishment. Personal training and nutrition advice can help tailor the plan to you.

move-record-session-01.text: Open Record a strength session, then check the exercises, sets, reps and weights before saving your record.

move-record-session-02.text: You can add it with yesterday's date. Use a reasonable estimate rather than inventing exact minutes you do not remember.

move-strength-basics-10.text: Their programme may not fit your experience or recovery. Use your own starting point and get guidance where you need it.

move-record-session-05.text: Yes. Give it a clear title and record the time you actually spent, if you want it in your history.

move-record-session-04.text: Save the steps you actually completed. The record is useful because it is honest, not because every box is filled.

move-record-session-03.text: Record the sets as accurately as the form allows. A note can preserve any detail that does not fit neatly.

move-record-session-06.text: Edit the saved entry and review the units and numbers before saving the correction.

move-record-session-08.text: Look at the previous records for the same exercise. Compare like with like, including the way you performed it.

move-record-session-07.text: No. A useful movement record can simply describe what you did and how long it took. No calorie estimate is required.

move-record-session-10.text: That needs your actual saved history. Open the relevant dates; this recording cannot verify a personal total.

move-record-session-09.text: Check the saved movement list before trying again, so you do not create a duplicate. If needed, keep a temporary note.

move-progress-gradually-01.text: Progress does not have to happen every session. Keep technique and recovery in view, and seek guidance on increases that suit you.

move-progress-gradually-04.text: Give the basics enough time. A movement you can control is a better starting point than a bigger number you cannot manage.

move-progress-gradually-02.text: Repeating a session can still be useful practice. Look at the longer pattern rather than demanding an improvement every time.

move-progress-gradually-03.text: When you are comfortable with the current version, ask a qualified coach about an appropriate next step. Avoid guessing through pain.

move-progress-gradually-05.text: A week may not tell you much. Look at consistency, context and comparable records over more time.

move-progress-gradually-07.text: I cannot guarantee a result or timeline. Training, nourishment, recovery and individual circumstances all affect what happens.

move-progress-gradually-06.text: Notice what has become easier or more controlled. Progress is not only an increase in the weight on the record.

move-progress-gradually-09.text: Use the routine's harder option only if it fits your ability and you understand the technique. You can keep the current version.

move-progress-gradually-08.text: A sudden jump is not necessary to make progress. Choose a manageable next session and build with appropriate guidance.

move-progress-gradually-10.text: One session can vary for many reasons. Record it honestly and look at the pattern before deciding something has gone wrong.

move-recovery-day-02.text: A streak is not more important than your wellbeing. Choose rest or a gentler option when that is what you need.

move-recovery-day-01.text: Rest can be part of training, not a break from being committed. Let today's plan reflect how you are doing.

move-recovery-day-03.text: Yes. You can move or rest without recording it. The app does not need evidence for every choice.

move-recovery-day-04.text: Consider a lighter day or rest. You do not need to repeat yesterday's effort just to feel consistent.

move-recovery-day-06.text: Choose a comfortable easy movement you already know, or simply rest. Recovery does not need its own demanding checklist.

move-recovery-day-08.text: That was a response to the day you had. Decide the next session when you know what capacity you have.

move-recovery-day-07.text: You can be frustrated and still respond kindly. The next useful step may be making recovery easier, not arguing with it.

move-recovery-day-09.text: Adding effort is not a substitute for recovery. Consider your rest and overall load, and get tailored advice if you are struggling.

move-recovery-day-10.text: Give rest its own place in the plan. You can describe it as recovery, or simply leave that space unfilled.

move-accessible-01.text: Your movement plan should fit your body. Choose suitable seated or supported options with guidance from a qualified professional where needed.

move-accessible-02.text: You can describe the activity you actually did in your movement journal. Walking is not the only movement worth recording.

move-accessible-04.text: Check the easier option and whether it is suitable for you. You can skip the movement if neither version fits.

move-accessible-03.text: You do not need to force the generic routine. Personalised advice can help identify movements that suit your access needs and health.

move-accessible-05.text: Read the next step before starting and pause whenever you need. The routine can wait for you.

move-accessible-06.text: Take another look at the current step. Understanding the movement matters more than keeping up with a timer.

move-accessible-07.text: Plan for that variation. Keep a smaller option available and seek tailored advice if you have a condition affecting activity.

move-accessible-10.text: You can focus on an activity, a skill, or how manageable it feels. A step count is only one possible measure.

move-accessible-08.text: Choose a safe, stable setup and guidance appropriate to you. Do not attempt an unsupported movement that feels unsafe.

move-accessible-09.text: That is useful information, not a failure. Choose an appropriate alternative or skip it; the routine should adapt to you.

move-kind-motivation-02.text: Then leave guilt out of the plan. Choose movement because it fits your needs today, not because you owe a punishment.

move-kind-motivation-03.text: Bounce can stay with your activity in Daywell. Choose quiet company or a little encouragement in the activity settings.

move-kind-motivation-01.text: You do not need to attack this session. Choose one comfortable beginning, and let that be enough to get moving.

move-kind-motivation-06.text: Try a small beginning and reassess. You are allowed to decide how much fits after you start.

move-kind-motivation-05.text: You could change one part you understand safely, or choose a different routine. Variety does not need to mean starting from zero.

move-kind-motivation-04.text: Choose A little encouragement or Stay quiet. The company can be there without interrupting every moment.

move-kind-motivation-08.text: You might move to feel a little more capable in everyday life. It does not have to be about changing your appearance.

move-kind-motivation-07.text: Think of an activity you like for its own sake. Music, a familiar route, or friendly company may make the choice easier.

move-kind-motivation-09.text: Your circumstances are real. Let the plan account for them instead of treating every difficulty as something to overpower.

move-with-people-02.text: Agree on a pace and activity that work for both of you. You do not need to turn shared time into a test.

move-kind-motivation-10.text: Start where you are today. A controlled, manageable effort is enough; you do not have to impress anyone here.

move-with-people-01.text: Try one simple invitation with a specific time. A short walk can be easier to arrange than a whole new fitness plan.

move-with-people-04.text: Make the invitation easy to answer: Would you like a short walk after lunch one day this week?

move-with-people-05.text: You can choose a smaller solo option or reschedule. Their cancellation does not have to decide every part of your plan.

move-with-people-03.text: Check the group's pace and expectations before joining. Finding a suitable group is more useful than forcing yourself to keep up.

move-with-people-06.text: You can choose movement on your own terms. A solo routine is just as valid a preference.

move-with-people-07.text: Choose your own load and technique. Training together does not mean your bodies or experience need identical numbers.

move-with-people-08.text: Choose an activity everyone can take part in comfortably. The shared experience can matter more than a training target.

move-with-people-09.text: That is useful information for a trainer. Ask for a version that fits your current ability and comfort.

move-with-people-10.text: Agree on what support you actually want, such as a friendly check-in. Make clear that rest and changed plans are allowed.

sleep-room-comfort-01.text: Start with one small change that matters to you: the light, a clear pillow, or somewhere to put the phone.

sleep-room-comfort-02.text: Adjust the bedding or room if you can. Comfort can be a practical change, not something you have to think your way into.

sleep-room-comfort-03.text: Work with what is possible. A small change to a light source may be enough to make the space more comfortable.

sleep-room-comfort-04.text: Take a moment to adjust your support. You can change position during a wind-down; staying still is not required.

sleep-room-comfort-05.text: Choose the parts you can influence, and discuss one useful adjustment if that feels possible. It does not have to be perfect.

sleep-room-comfort-06.text: A small visual boundary may help mark the end of work. Cover the screen or put work materials out of immediate view.

sleep-room-comfort-07.text: You can keep it nearby without keeping the feed open. Place it screen-down and preserve any contacts you need to hear.

sleep-room-comfort-08.text: A helpful routine does not require special purchases. Start with comfort and changes available in the room you already have.

sleep-room-comfort-09.text: Bring one familiar part of your routine into this space, if you can. A known sound or small ritual may make it feel more settled.

sleep-room-comfort-10.text: I cannot change the room, but you can choose what sound to add or remove. Daywell's soft rustling is optional.

move-travelling-01.text: The no-equipment routines can give you options. Check the space and choose what feels suitable after the journey.

move-travelling-02.text: When it is safe and practical, change position or take a gentle movement break. Stay aware of the train and people around you.

move-travelling-03.text: Wait until you are safely parked. Then choose a comfortable change of position and gentle movement without forcing a stretch.

move-travelling-04.text: Open Hotel room fifteen in Move and review the exercises. Adapt or skip anything that does not fit the room or your body.

move-travelling-05.text: Choose an activity that is safe with the footwear and surroundings you have. You do not need to improvise a risky workout.

move-travelling-06.text: You can let the holiday have a different rhythm. Notice ordinary movement without recreating every usual workout.

move-travelling-08.text: Once safely parked, choose a safe place to walk or change position. Keep clear of traffic and return when you feel ready.

move-travelling-09.text: Use a manageable first session and see how it feels. You do not need to make up every missed activity.

move-travelling-07.text: Start with rest and comfort. You can choose gentle movement when it feels appropriate, rather than forcing the usual session.

move-learning-form-02.text: Use a controlled pace you have learned for the exercise. Speed is not a substitute for understanding the movement.

move-learning-form-01.text: Pause the routine and read it again. If the movement is still unclear, get a qualified demonstration rather than guessing.

move-travelling-10.text: This MVP does not automatically track your travel activity. You can add a movement record yourself when you want one.

move-learning-form-03.text: Put technique first. A simple counter or note can help, but the number does not need to override control.

move-learning-form-04.text: A clear demonstration from a qualified source can help. Daywell's text cue alone may not be enough for an unfamiliar exercise.

move-learning-form-05.text: Stop and reset. Ask a qualified coach about breathing and technique appropriate to that lift rather than pushing through discomfort.

move-learning-form-07.text: That detail depends on the exercise and your body. Get a clear demonstration before adding resistance or speed.

move-learning-form-06.text: Understand the easier version first. Choose difficulty that matches your skill, not just the version that looks impressive.

move-learning-form-10.text: Pause before continuing. You can reduce the demand and return to a version you can control, or end the session.

move-learning-form-09.text: That is a useful intention. Keep the effort manageable and notice whether the movement feels more controlled.

move-timer-company-01.text: Review the proposed walk and duration before starting. Keep Daywell open if you want the timer and companion cues.

move-timer-company-03.text: Choose Resume activity or Continue on the routine timer. Review the remaining time before carrying on.

move-timer-company-02.text: Use Pause activity or the routine's Pause button. Check the on-screen timer to confirm it has stopped.

move-timer-company-04.text: Choose Stay quiet for the activity's company level. You can keep the illustration without spoken check-ins.

move-timer-company-07.text: Use Timers or choose quiet company. You do not need motivational prompts to keep time.

move-timer-company-06.text: The browser may pause when the phone is locked. Use your device's timer for something that must work in the background.

move-timer-company-05.text: You can end the activity now. If you save a record, use what you actually did rather than the original planned duration.

move-timer-company-09.text: End the incorrect activity, then review the right title and duration before starting again.

move-timer-company-08.text: A finished timer does not prove what movement happened. Review and save the activity details yourself.

move-timer-company-10.text: Check the activity controls before changing the plan. Keep the saved record separate from what you originally intended.

move-returning-01.text: Begin with what fits today. There is no exercise debt to repay before you are allowed to return.

move-returning-02.text: Look for the part that repeatedly becomes difficult. A smaller or more flexible plan may be easier to return to.

move-returning-03.text: The earlier movement still happened. Adjust the next step to your current life instead of trying to recreate a different week.

move-returning-06.text: Choose something manageable on an ordinary day, with an even smaller version for difficult days.

move-returning-04.text: You can quietly choose one session. A fresh start does not need a public promise or a complete new identity.

move-returning-05.text: The rest of the week is still available. Choose the next practical opportunity without making Monday decide everything.

move-returning-09.text: You do not need a lifetime promise to choose today. Make the next step useful even if the pattern changes later.

move-returning-08.text: Caring can take real energy. Begin with a small activity that fits your current responsibilities and leaves room for your own rest.

move-returning-07.text: Look at what changed around you. A fair comparison includes time, health, responsibilities and the opportunities you actually had.

move-returning-10.text: Returning is worth noticing. Keep the celebration gentle and let the next session stay manageable.

eat-choosing-meal-01.text: Let's make the choice smaller. Would something warm or something cold feel easier tonight?

eat-choosing-meal-03.text: Choose one familiar place, then one meal you usually enjoy. You can stop comparing once that choice is made.

eat-choosing-meal-04.text: Toast with eggs, beans, or another topping you enjoy can be a starting point. Add something fresh if it is available.

eat-choosing-meal-02.text: Start with the easiest ingredient you have. It only needs to become a manageable meal, not an exciting one.

eat-choosing-meal-07.text: Pick something familiar that fits what you have. Lunch does not have to be the best possible choice.

eat-choosing-meal-06.text: Let's choose between two: a simple pasta meal or a filled sandwich. Which sounds more manageable?

eat-choosing-meal-05.text: A filled wrap or a simple sandwich can keep the dishes down. Choose a filling that suits your needs.

eat-choosing-meal-08.text: Could you share one base, like rice or bread, and let people choose their own toppings?

eat-choosing-meal-10.text: Tell me a few ingredients you have and any dietary needs. We can then narrow the options together.

eat-choosing-meal-09.text: An assembled meal counts. Put together a few ready to eat foods you like, without turning it into a cooking project.

eat-quick-options-02.text: Try preparing something portable that you enjoy, such as overnight oats or a filled roll, when you have a moment.

eat-quick-options-03.text: You can still have a meal. Ready to eat ingredients and prepared food are useful options on a day like this.

eat-quick-options-01.text: Use that time for something straightforward to eat. A sandwich or leftovers may be enough to get lunch started.

eat-quick-options-05.text: A bowl of cereal, soup, or a simple rice meal could work. Start with food; the rest can wait.

eat-quick-options-04.text: Frozen vegetables, tinned pulses, and ready prepared ingredients can reduce the preparation. Choose what works for your kitchen.

eat-quick-options-06.text: Yes. Frozen ingredients and prepared meals can be useful parts of everyday eating. Follow the preparation instructions.

eat-quick-options-07.text: Keep the decision gentle. A familiar, easy meal is enough tonight; it does not need extra steps.

eat-quick-options-09.text: See whether you can protect a few minutes to eat now, and make room for more food later if you need it.

eat-quick-options-08.text: Look for food you can use safely as it is, or cook from frozen if the label allows it. You can change the plan.

eat-quick-options-10.text: Choose one shelf or freezer meal you already like. Keep its ingredients together so there is less to think about.

eat-cupboard-options-02.text: Think of rice as the base. Check for a suitable topping, some vegetables, and a sauce or seasoning you enjoy.

eat-cupboard-options-01.text: That can be a simple starting point. If you have beans, lentils, or another protein you enjoy, you could add some.

eat-cupboard-options-04.text: Before your next shop, take a quick look at one cupboard and the fridge. A short list can be enough.

eat-cupboard-options-03.text: Tell me which vegetables you have and whether they are still fresh. We can find a simple way to use them.

eat-cupboard-options-05.text: Pick one familiar meal, then check only for its ingredients. You do not need to organise every cupboard first.

eat-cupboard-options-07.text: A photo may miss labels, dates, and ingredients. Tell me what is there and any food restrictions before we choose.

eat-cupboard-options-06.text: Choose one item you can safely use this week. Build a meal around that before adding anything new.

eat-cupboard-options-08.text: Choose one to use soon. Check reliable storage or freezing guidance for the others, so you do not have to rush through everything.

eat-food-shopping-01.text: Open your food shopping list to add milk. This recording cannot save the item for you.

eat-cupboard-options-10.text: I cannot confirm food safety from a description alone. Storage time, temperature, and the food itself all matter.

eat-cupboard-options-09.text: Check its label and reliable food safety guidance. If you cannot establish that it is safe, choose something else.

eat-food-shopping-03.text: Start with three meals you know you will eat. Reusing a few ingredients can make the list shorter.

eat-food-shopping-02.text: First choose the meal and check what you already have. The remaining ingredients can go on your food shopping list.

eat-food-shopping-04.text: A short list grouped by section may help. You can shop for a few days instead of solving the whole week.

eat-food-shopping-07.text: You can remove bread in the food shopping list. Check the right item before deleting it.

eat-food-shopping-05.text: Write the meal name beside its ingredients. Before leaving, check the list against what you already have.

eat-food-shopping-06.text: Your saved list needs to be opened before its items can be read. A prepared recording cannot know what is on it.

eat-food-shopping-08.text: Choose food for your next few meals and one easy backup. A shorter list is a valid plan.

eat-food-shopping-09.text: Try starting with meals you realistically expect to make. Leave room for convenience, rather than planning an ambitious week.

eat-food-shopping-10.text: Daywell does not place grocery orders. You can use your food list as a reference when ordering from your chosen shop.

eat-flexible-planning-02.text: Try a small set of options rather than fixed meals for every day. You can choose based on your energy.

eat-flexible-planning-01.text: Plan just one meal ahead. You can repeat something familiar and leave the rest of the week open.

eat-flexible-planning-03.text: Repeating a lunch you enjoy can simplify things. Aim for variety across your eating over time, without making each meal complicated.

eat-flexible-planning-05.text: Meals with separate toppings or sides can offer choice without several completely different dinners.

eat-flexible-planning-04.text: Include a quick backup meal and keep some ingredients flexible. A plan can support your day without controlling it.

eat-flexible-planning-06.text: Choose one useful preparation step, such as washing produce or making a portion for later. You can stop there.

eat-flexible-planning-09.text: Think about when you will be home and when you will be out. Choose one realistic food option for each part of the day.

eat-flexible-planning-07.text: That tells you the plan asked for too much this week. Try fewer cooking nights and more easy options next time.

eat-breakfast-start-02.text: Could you take something with you for later? Make space for food in a way that fits your morning.

eat-breakfast-start-01.text: Make it as familiar as possible. Keep an easy option where you can find it without searching.

eat-flexible-planning-10.text: Keep a few adaptable ingredients available if you can. The plan can be a set of possibilities rather than a promise.

eat-breakfast-start-03.text: Cereal, yoghurt with fruit, or a sandwich could be options, depending on what you enjoy and can eat.

eat-breakfast-start-04.text: Porridge or toast with a familiar topping can be a simple option. Follow the preparation instructions for what you use.

eat-breakfast-start-05.text: Put a gentle reminder beside something you already do in the morning. Keep the food choice easy.

eat-breakfast-start-07.text: Breakfast does not need special breakfast food. Safely stored and reheated leftovers can be an option you enjoy.

eat-breakfast-start-06.text: You do not have to force a large meal. Start with something manageable, and seek advice if low appetite keeps making eating difficult.

eat-breakfast-start-08.text: Look for simple food you can store safely, or check what the hotel offers. You can keep the choice familiar.

eat-breakfast-start-09.text: Change one part, such as the fruit or topping, before replacing the whole routine.

eat-breakfast-start-10.text: Choose an option that stores safely overnight. Set out what you need so the morning has fewer steps.

eat-lunch-pause-01.text: Could you protect a short break to eat today? Your work can have a pause without needing to be finished first.

eat-lunch-pause-03.text: Choose food you can keep at a safe temperature. A suitable container and storage plan matter as much as the recipe.

eat-lunch-pause-04.text: If it is possible, close the messages for the first few bites. Give yourself one small part of the break back.

eat-lunch-pause-02.text: Look for one accessible option nearby or at home. You can solve today's lunch without fixing the whole routine.

eat-lunch-pause-05.text: Is there another suitable place where you could eat more comfortably? You can choose a quieter break when circumstances allow.

eat-lunch-pause-07.text: A sandwich, filled wrap, or suitable cold meal could work. Make sure you can store it safely until lunchtime.

eat-lunch-pause-06.text: A visible lunch reminder may help interrupt the rush. Keep a practical food option ready for when the reminder appears.

eat-lunch-pause-10.text: Eating is an ordinary need. A lunch break does not have to be earned by getting through the whole list.

eat-lunch-pause-09.text: Leftovers can make lunch easier. Check how they were stored and follow safe reheating guidance where needed.

eat-lunch-pause-08.text: Use a reminder you can verify in your calendar or alarm tool. This recording does not create a notification.

eat-evening-meals-01.text: Sit down for a moment if you need to. Then choose the easiest available meal, with as few steps as possible.

eat-evening-meals-03.text: One food choice does not define how you look after yourself. Notice what made cooking difficult and plan a useful backup.

eat-evening-meals-02.text: You can use prepared ingredients, repeat meals, or choose something ready made. Dinner does not need to become a second shift.

eat-evening-meals-06.text: Clear just enough space to prepare something safely. The whole kitchen does not need to be finished before you eat.

eat-evening-meals-05.text: You can make the meal pleasant for yourself too. Choose somewhere comfortable and food that fits the evening you have.

eat-evening-meals-04.text: Think of a familiar meal you enjoy. Comfort can come from something simple, warm, and easy to settle with.

eat-evening-meals-07.text: Choose the meal, gather only its ingredients, then follow its cooking instructions. Keep tonight's choice simple.

eat-evening-meals-09.text: A small, familiar meal is enough. You are allowed convenience even when you are the only person eating.

eat-evening-meals-08.text: Pause and make the kitchen safe first. You can switch to an easier meal; the original plan does not need rescuing at any cost.

eat-snack-options-01.text: Try something you enjoy and can eat comfortably, such as fruit, toast, or yoghurt. Check it suits your dietary needs.

eat-evening-meals-10.text: Choose the meal before tomorrow gets busy. Check its ingredients and any safe preparation you can do ahead.

eat-snack-options-02.text: Snacks can be part of everyday eating. You do not need to turn having something to eat into a moral decision.

eat-snack-options-04.text: Would you prefer something crunchy or something soft? One small choice can narrow it down.

eat-snack-options-03.text: Choose food that travels and stores safely. Keep it easy to reach when you are stopped somewhere safe to eat.

eat-snack-options-05.text: You can have something to eat while dinner is being prepared. You do not have to wait until you are uncomfortable.

eat-snack-options-07.text: Look for food with suitable storage instructions and packaging. Keep a couple of options you actually like.

eat-snack-options-06.text: At your next safe opportunity, look for an accessible food option. Taking care of that need is part of the journey.

eat-snack-options-08.text: Try describing what happened without blame. If food worries keep taking over, support from a qualified professional may help.

eat-protein-options-01.text: Beans, lentils, tofu, eggs, dairy, fish, and meat are examples. Choose options that fit your preferences and dietary needs.

eat-snack-options-09.text: Enjoyment can be part of eating. You can think about the overall pattern without labelling a single food choice as a failure.

eat-protein-options-04.text: Regular meals, enough food overall, and suitable protein sources can support training. A personalised plan depends on your needs.

eat-protein-options-02.text: Beans, lentils, tofu, and other plant foods can contribute protein. A varied eating pattern can help you include different nutrients.

eat-protein-options-06.text: You could add beans, tofu, egg, fish, or another suitable food you enjoy to a familiar lunch.

eat-protein-options-09.text: You do not need food marketed for the gym. Everyday ingredients can be useful, including beans, lentils, and other affordable options.

eat-protein-options-08.text: A workable eating routine matters more than making every plate feel perfect. Leave room for ordinary meals and enjoyment.

eat-regular-rhythm-02.text: Keep one reliable, easy food option available. The backup can support you when the usual routine does not fit.

eat-regular-rhythm-01.text: Try placing an eating break beside a regular part of your day. A visible reminder can help you notice the time.

eat-regular-rhythm-03.text: Choose one supportive habit rather than a strict list of restrictions. Make it something you can adapt when life changes.

eat-regular-rhythm-06.text: Put a note beside your keys or bag, and prepare what you can safely in advance. Keep the reminder visible.

eat-regular-rhythm-05.text: You do not have to make the day perfect again. Think about your next practical opportunity to eat something.

eat-regular-rhythm-08.text: You can use a simple reminder such as, have I made room to eat? No calorie target is needed for that prompt.

eat-regular-rhythm-07.text: Try planning around events, like leaving home or finishing a shift, instead of relying only on fixed meal times.

eat-less-judgement-01.text: One meal is not a verdict on you. You can continue your day without punishing yourself or trying to undo it.

eat-regular-rhythm-10.text: Start by identifying the part of the day when eating is hardest. We can make one small change around that moment.

eat-less-judgement-02.text: Dessert does not mean you have lost permission to eat dinner. If these rules feel persistent, reach out for qualified support.

eat-less-judgement-04.text: Other people's plates do not show their needs or their whole day. Bring the focus back to what supports your own eating.

eat-less-judgement-03.text: I will not use shame around food. We can look for a small, practical change that respects your needs.

eat-less-judgement-05.text: You can step away from tracking. If anxiety around food is growing, a qualified professional can help you find a gentler approach.

eat-less-judgement-07.text: I would rather help you describe what a meal offers and what you enjoy. Moral labels can make eating feel harder.

eat-less-judgement-06.text: You can focus on regular meals, enjoyment, and having energy for your day. A weight goal is not required.

eat-budget-meals-01.text: Start with affordable foods you already use. Tinned and frozen options can help you build meals without needing speciality products.

eat-budget-meals-02.text: Choose one lunch you could bring from home this week. Repeating an easy option can reduce both cost and decisions.

eat-budget-meals-03.text: Tell me your budget, what food you already have, and where you shop. Prices vary, so we would need to check the actual costs.

eat-budget-meals-04.text: Buy for fewer planned meals at a time if you can. Choose ingredients that work in more than one familiar dish.

eat-budget-meals-06.text: Beans can go into a jacket potato, a wrap, or a simple tomato sauce. Use the preparation directions on the label.

eat-budget-meals-07.text: Your time, equipment, and energy matter too. Choose the combination of prepared and homemade food that works in your circumstances.

eat-budget-meals-05.text: You do not need to make organic food a requirement. Work with food that is accessible, affordable, and suitable for you.

eat-budget-meals-10.text: Current prices need a live check. A saved recording cannot compare today's offers, but your shopping list can help organise the comparison.

eat-budget-meals-09.text: You deserve help with that. A local council, food support organisation, or trusted community service may be able to connect you with food.

eat-budget-meals-08.text: Choose a simpler recipe or check which substitutions are suitable. A shorter ingredient list may fit your budget better.

eat-notes-and-logs-02.text: Your food history needs to be opened to answer that. A prerecorded reply cannot see yesterday's entries.

eat-notes-and-logs-01.text: Open the food log and add the sandwich there. Check the saved entry so your record reflects what you intended.

eat-notes-and-logs-03.text: A photo cannot provide an exact calorie count. Portions, ingredients, and preparation can be unclear, so estimates should be treated as uncertain.

eat-notes-and-logs-04.text: You can add a note later if it is useful. Your record does not need to be complete to offer something helpful.

eat-notes-and-logs-05.text: A simple note about meals can be enough. You do not need to record every ingredient or calorie for that purpose.

eat-notes-and-logs-06.text: Find the entry in your food history and check its details before removing it. This audio does not delete saved data.

eat-notes-and-logs-07.text: Write its name and the part you liked. That can become a useful option when choosing a future meal.

eat-notes-and-logs-08.text: Check Daywell's current privacy information and settings before adding sensitive details. Only share what you are comfortable recording.

eat-notes-and-logs-09.text: That would need your actual records and a clear idea of what improvement means to you. A saved reply cannot assess the pattern.

eat-notes-and-logs-10.text: Keep only the details that help you. You can pause logging when it stops feeling useful.

focus-starting-friction-01.text: Make the first action smaller than the task. Opening the document or finding one item can be the whole beginning.

focus-starting-friction-02.text: Write one rough sentence about what the document needs to do. It can be a note to yourself, not the finished opening.

focus-starting-friction-03.text: Begin with the recipient and a plain subject line. Then write the main point in words you can edit later.

focus-starting-friction-04.text: Choose one small transition that feels possible, such as putting your feet on the floor. You can decide the next step after that.

focus-starting-friction-07.text: Choose one small surface or one kind of item. Stop before the task spreads to the whole room.

focus-starting-friction-05.text: Name only the next visible action. You do not need to hold the whole project in mind to take that step.

focus-starting-friction-06.text: You can use a short focus timer for company. Pick one tiny action to try while it runs, with no need to impress anyone.

focus-starting-friction-08.text: The next few minutes are still available. Choose a small action that fits the time you have now.

focus-starting-friction-09.text: Open the material and find the section you need. That is enough for the first step; reading can come next.

focus-starting-friction-10.text: Try a small experiment: give the task two minutes of imperfect attention. You can reassess when those minutes are over.

focus-choose-priority-03.text: That needs your actual task list and deadlines. Open the list so you can compare what matters most today.

focus-choose-priority-01.text: Check which task has a real deadline or consequence today. Start there, and let the rest wait on the list.

focus-choose-priority-02.text: Choose one thing that would make today more manageable. You can keep the other priorities visible without doing them together.

focus-choose-priority-06.text: Check how much time and energy the evening actually has. Choose a smaller set and leave some room to rest.

focus-choose-priority-04.text: Give the important task a very small opening, such as gathering its materials. You do not need to finish it in one go.

focus-choose-priority-05.text: Look for a real deadline, someone depending on it, or a practical consequence. Tasks without those may have more room.

focus-choose-priority-08.text: Before adding it, check what would need to move. You can ask which existing task should take lower priority.

focus-choose-priority-09.text: Compare their deadlines and what each one would unblock. If they are genuinely equal, choose the easier starting point.

focus-choose-priority-07.text: The list can hold possibilities rather than demands. Pick what realistically fits today and move the rest out of view.

focus-distracted-again-02.text: Choose the one tab needed for the next step. Save the others for later if you are worried about losing them.

focus-distracted-again-01.text: You noticed now. Put it somewhere a little less convenient, then return to one small part of what you were doing.

focus-choose-priority-10.text: Choose the task you want to prioritise and save it in the app. This recording cannot update the priority itself.

focus-distracted-again-05.text: If your responsibilities allow it, choose a later check in time. Close the messages for one short focus period.

focus-distracted-again-03.text: You can return five times too. Each return is a new chance to make the task smaller or the environment easier.

focus-distracted-again-04.text: Keep a small place to park those tasks. Write a few words, then come back to the action in front of you.

focus-distracted-again-07.text: Move just the things that compete with the next task. You do not need a perfectly tidy desk to continue.

focus-distracted-again-08.text: Look for the last small thing you completed. Write a brief note about the next action, then begin there.

focus-distracted-again-06.text: Could you change location, reduce one sound, or choose a task that needs less concentration for now?

focus-distracted-again-10.text: A distraction does not cancel the work you have done. Take one gentle return to the next visible step.

focus-distracted-again-09.text: Daywell does not automatically block other apps. Your device may have focus or screen time settings you can choose to use.

focus-break-it-down-01.text: Choose one category first, such as clothes. Put those in their places before deciding whether to take on anything else.

focus-break-it-down-03.text: Find the time and location, then gather what you need to bring. Add any questions you want to remember.

focus-break-it-down-02.text: List the headings, put rough notes beneath them, then work on one section. Editing can be a separate pass.

focus-break-it-down-04.text: Start with the essentials you cannot easily replace. Then choose clothing for the actual days and activities ahead.

focus-break-it-down-07.text: Describe a clear stopping point in one sentence. Aim for that version before adding extra work.

focus-break-it-down-05.text: Write why you are calling and one sentence to open with. Keep any details you might need beside you.

focus-break-it-down-06.text: List the next action for each part, then choose one that unblocks something else. You can leave the full plan on paper.

focus-break-it-down-09.text: Keep a separate note for extra ideas. Return to the stopping point you originally chose.

focus-break-it-down-08.text: That needs the project details and a confirmed task list. Review the steps before saving them in your planning tools.

focus-break-it-down-10.text: Read the heading or last note, then write one rough point. Keep the next action concrete and small.

focus-timer-requests-02.text: Use the pause control on your current timer. This prepared reply cannot pause a running session for you.

focus-timer-requests-01.text: Open the focus timer, choose five minutes, and press start. Check that it is running before beginning.

focus-timer-requests-03.text: The remaining time needs to be read from the active timer. Open it to check the current countdown.

focus-timer-requests-04.text: Choose a duration that fits your energy today. A short session can still create a useful beginning.

focus-timer-requests-05.text: You can work without a countdown or choose a gentler stopping point. The tool should support you, not add pressure.

focus-timer-requests-06.text: Yes. You can stop when you need to and record what helped. Finishing a countdown is not a test of your worth.

focus-timer-requests-08.text: You can end the session there. Take a small pause before deciding whether another task belongs in this block.

focus-timer-requests-09.text: You can choose a little more time, while checking your other needs and commitments. The timer is a guide.

focus-timer-requests-07.text: Use the reset control and confirm the duration before starting again. Make sure you intend to clear the current countdown.

focus-interruption-plan-01.text: Write the next small action you remember. If that is unclear, review the last thing you completed and start from there.

focus-interruption-plan-02.text: Leave a brief note saying where you are and what comes next. That can make returning less demanding.

focus-timer-requests-10.text: Do not rely on an in app timer as a guaranteed wake up alarm. Use and test a suitable device alarm for that.

focus-interruption-plan-04.text: Take a moment to look at your workspace. The open material or last note may show the next step.

focus-interruption-plan-03.text: Could you ask for one short protected period, or switch to work that tolerates interruptions for now?

focus-interruption-plan-05.text: Pause before responding if you can. Then explain the practical thing you need, such as a few minutes to finish a step.

focus-interruption-plan-06.text: You could say, I am finishing one thing; can I come back to you in a few minutes?

focus-interruption-plan-07.text: Choose tasks that can be left safely at a clear stopping point. Your plan needs room for the responsibilities you have.

focus-interruption-plan-08.text: Add a short note in the relevant task or journal entry, then check it saved. A recording cannot store that note itself.

focus-interruption-plan-09.text: Write any small part you still remember. If it does not return now, you can leave space and come back later.

focus-interruption-plan-10.text: Start with a brief review of what is still relevant. Choose one current action instead of trying to catch up on everything.

focus-task-transitions-01.text: Close one work item and leave a note for tomorrow. Then choose a small physical change, like putting your bag away.

focus-task-transitions-03.text: Give the first task a small ending. Then name only the first action of the next one.

focus-task-transitions-04.text: You can use that gap to settle, prepare, or simply pause. It does not need to become another work session.

focus-task-transitions-02.text: Choose a clear stopping action now. Save the work, note the next step, and close the tool if your responsibilities allow it.

focus-task-transitions-07.text: Write the next question or page to return to. Leave a clear starting point for your next session.

focus-task-transitions-05.text: Let there be a short pause. Then choose from a small set: rest, an ordinary need, or the next priority.

focus-task-transitions-06.text: Return to the essentials for leaving. Extra tasks can go on a note instead of coming with you into this moment.

focus-task-transitions-09.text: Let arriving be a separate moment. Put down what you are carrying and notice that the journey has finished.

focus-task-transitions-10.text: Note anything that genuinely needs carrying forward. Then choose one sign that work is finished for now.

focus-task-transitions-08.text: Clear a little space, choose one task, and decide a stopping point. Keep the ritual short enough to be useful.

focus-imperfect-work-02.text: Leave a rough opening and move to the next point. The beginning may be easier to edit once the rest exists.

focus-imperfect-work-03.text: Look for a small, reversible next step. You can build in a check without needing certainty before every action.

focus-imperfect-work-01.text: Check it against the actual requirements. If those are met, choose one final review rather than an endless search for certainty.

focus-imperfect-work-05.text: Return to what this task needs from you today. Other people's finished work does not show their drafts.

focus-imperfect-work-06.text: Keep the plan you have and test one small step. What happens next can inform the next part of the plan.

focus-imperfect-work-04.text: Choose the minimum setup the task needs. Let the first small action happen before making more improvements.

focus-imperfect-work-08.text: Check what still needs changing against a clear standard. If it meets the need, consider calling that version complete.

focus-imperfect-work-07.text: A rough draft is a useful stage of work. Its job is to give you something to shape, not to impress.

focus-imperfect-work-09.text: I cannot guarantee an outcome from a prepared reply. A review needs the work itself and the criteria it will be judged against.

focus-life-admin-01.text: Choose one envelope and a place to put it. You only need to find out what that one item needs next.

focus-life-admin-02.text: Read just the first section and gather what it asks for. Complete one part before looking at the whole form again.

focus-imperfect-work-10.text: Time can reflect many things, including the task and your circumstances. Choose a useful next step without turning the clock into a judgement.

focus-life-admin-05.text: Pick one with a real deadline. Put the others in one visible list so they do not all need to stay in your head.

focus-life-admin-03.text: Write down the booking details and choose a time to contact them. Verify any reminder you create.

focus-life-admin-04.text: Daywell cannot make that booking through a saved audio reply. Contact your provider through its booking system.

focus-life-admin-07.text: List only what tomorrow requires. Gather those items into one place and check the essentials before adding anything extra.

focus-life-admin-08.text: Sending an email needs the message, recipient, and an actual sending tool. This recording cannot send it.

focus-life-admin-06.text: Open the information when you feel able, and note the actual amount and deadline. For debt advice, use a qualified support service.

focus-study-support-01.text: Pause and ask what the paragraph is trying to say. Write one rough sentence in your own words, then check it against the text.

focus-life-admin-09.text: Find out what action is still possible now. A practical message or next step may help more than replaying the mistake.

focus-life-admin-10.text: Choose one manageable job for today and make its first step obvious. You do not need to fix the whole backlog at once.

focus-study-support-02.text: Choose one topic and one small question about it. Start by seeing what you can recall before checking your notes.

focus-study-support-03.text: Choose the most useful topics for the time left, and leave room for ordinary needs and sleep. Avoid trying to cover everything perfectly.

focus-study-support-04.text: A quiet study group or a trusted person working nearby may help. You can also use a short timer to give the session a shape.

focus-study-support-05.text: Pick one resource for the next question. Keep the others available for a specific gap instead of moving between all of them.

focus-study-support-07.text: Check whether a break or stopping for the day would be more useful. More time at the desk is not always more learning.

focus-study-support-06.text: Tell me the topic and the part that is confusing. A useful explanation needs that context rather than a generic recording.

focus-study-support-09.text: Write the next topic and one question to start with. That gives your next session a place to begin.

focus-study-support-10.text: I can support practice and understanding, but I cannot take an exam on your behalf. We can work on the topic you need to learn.

focus-study-support-08.text: Try one small recall question and then check your notes. Begin with a narrow topic rather than testing yourself on everything.

progress-gentle-review-01.text: Your saved history can help you look back. Choose one thing that supported you and one thing you would like to make easier.

progress-gentle-review-02.text: Describe what happened before deciding what it means. Include your circumstances, your effort, and any support you had.

progress-gentle-review-03.text: Think of one moment that felt useful, kind, or manageable. It can be ordinary and still belong in your reflection.

progress-gentle-review-06.text: Try this: what made today a little easier, and would I like to make room for it again?

progress-gentle-review-04.text: A monthly summary needs your actual saved entries. Open your history and choose the period you want to review.

progress-gentle-review-05.text: Look for small records: an appointment attended, a meal made, a walk, or a moment of rest. Progress can be quiet.

progress-gentle-review-07.text: Yes. Your history can include difficult days without needing a positive ending. A plain note is enough.

progress-gentle-review-08.text: Take a second look at what you did carry through, including ordinary care and responsibilities that may be easy to overlook.

progress-gentle-review-09.text: Name one helpful thing, one difficult thing, and one small adjustment for next week. You can stop after those three.

progress-gaps-return-01.text: You can start with today. There is no backlog of app visits you need to catch up on.

progress-gentle-review-10.text: Write a few words about the day as it was. Your record can hold experience as well as completed tasks.

progress-gaps-return-02.text: Empty spaces mean there is no entry, not that nothing happened. You can leave those spaces as they are.

progress-gaps-return-04.text: Only if it is useful to you. A record can be helpful without being complete.

progress-gaps-return-05.text: There is no explanation you owe the app. Choose one thing that would help you today.

progress-gaps-return-03.text: The earlier effort still happened. Choose a version of the routine that fits where you are now.

progress-gaps-return-07.text: Look at what got in the way this time. A smaller step or a different cue may fit better than a stronger promise.

progress-gaps-return-08.text: Your circumstances may have changed. Begin with what is manageable now rather than demanding the old routine immediately.

progress-gaps-return-06.text: An empty day does not prove you did nothing. Review the available history controls if you want to change how entries are shown.

progress-small-wins-01.text: Give that moment a little room. You took a step that had been difficult to begin.

progress-gaps-return-09.text: A return can be useful in itself. You noticed a need and chose to respond to it again.

progress-gaps-return-10.text: You can choose a new intention for today while keeping your earlier records. The past can stay without directing every next step.

progress-small-wins-03.text: You noticed what you needed and responded. That is a useful moment to remember.

progress-small-wins-02.text: That was part of caring for yourself today. You can acknowledge it without comparing it with someone else's day.

progress-small-wins-04.text: You made space for something different. Notice what the walk was like, without needing it to become a bigger achievement.

progress-small-wins-06.text: Asking for support can take effort. You do not have to manage every difficulty on your own.

progress-small-wins-07.text: You made an ending to the workday. Let the time you protected be available for what you need now.

progress-small-wins-05.text: You made one meal happen. If it helped, note what made it manageable so you can return to it.

progress-small-wins-09.text: Add a note to your history or journal and check it saved. The recording itself cannot create that entry.

progress-small-wins-08.text: You paid attention to your circumstances. Recovery and rest can belong alongside movement.

progress-small-wins-10.text: A quiet acknowledgement is enough: that took some effort, and you did it. Nothing more needs to be made of it.

progress-notice-patterns-01.text: Look at what Mondays ask of you. A smaller plan or a little preparation may help more than blaming yourself.

progress-notice-patterns-02.text: A brief note about the day may help you notice patterns over time. Avoid treating one entry as the whole explanation.

progress-notice-patterns-06.text: Company may be a useful support. You can plan with that in mind instead of treating it as a weakness.

progress-notice-patterns-04.text: That is worth noticing. Think about what part of going out helps and whether a manageable version fits another day.

progress-notice-patterns-05.text: The scrolling may be filling a need for a low effort pause. Try keeping another easy resting option available.

progress-notice-patterns-08.text: That gives you a practical place to adjust. Could you protect a food break or keep an accessible backup option?

progress-notice-patterns-09.text: Look for differences in circumstances as well as activities. Ask what helped, rather than which week deserves a higher score.

progress-calendar-ahead-01.text: Open tomorrow in your calendar to see the saved plans. A prerecorded reply cannot read your current schedule.

progress-calendar-ahead-02.text: Choose Friday and add the walk with the time you want. Check the saved date so it appears where you expect.

progress-notice-patterns-10.text: You do not need one perfect explanation. Choose a small change you can observe, and seek professional help for persistent health concerns.

progress-calendar-ahead-03.text: Open the scheduled workout and choose its new date. Review the change before saving it.

progress-calendar-ahead-05.text: You can add a rest block to your calendar. Give it enough room to feel like a pause, rather than another performance.
